 The Trump administration proposed narrowing who’s eligible to receive federal food assistance, a change that officials estimate could block 6.3 million people from using the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. 
 The proposed rule released Monday would limit automatic eligibility for SNAP benefits, formerly known as food stamps, to low-income households that receive cash assistance from the federally-funded Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program . Households using what the rule describes as non-cash or nominal TANF services would no longer automatically qualify. 
 The draft, which estimates the change would save $44.6 billion between fiscal 2027 and 2031, is the Trump administration’s latest effort to curb SNAP spending, citing concerns the program is rife with wasted resources and fraud. It also follows a law Republican lawmakers enacted in 2025 that slashed federal spending on the nation’s primary anti-hunger program, tightened eligibility, and bolstered work requirements; participation fell by about 5.5 million people in the year since, federal data shows. 
 The US Department of Agriculture’s proposal targets a policy called “broad-based categorical eligibility,” which lets states provide TANF benefits such as childcare or workforce training to effectively bypass SNAP’s income eligibility limit. 
 In 2024, nearly $214 million in SNAP benefits went to households that wouldn’t have met the program’s income or resource limits without TANF-driven categorical eligibility, according to the proposal. 
 “This spending does not align with Congress’ intent or the Secretary’s guiding principle to support policy options that protect both truly needy recipients and the American taxpayer,” the proposed rule said. 
 The first Trump administration attempted to revise categorical eligibility rules in 2019 , but the Biden administration withdrew that proposed rule in 2021. The number of states leveraging this policy more than doubled from 18 to 43 under the Obama administration — today that number is up to 46, according to the proposed rule. 
 Expanding SNAP eligibility using broad-based categorical standards “may threaten the integrity of the program by eroding public trust that SNAP benefits are available only to those who meet the eligibility limits set in law,” the proposed rule said.
 The rule, if finalized, is expected to take full effect in fiscal 2029. USDA officials are soliciting comments on the proposal for 30 days after it’s published in the Federal Register.
